cards.a: Every device connects to exactly two neighbors, forming a closed loop. Frames travel in one direction (token ring / FDDI) around the ring. Physically, modern rings are often implemented as a 'ring-of-stars' where each node is a hub/switch and the hubs form the logical ring.

cards.q: What is the difference between a logical ring and a physical star-ring?
cards.a: A logical ring means data circulates in a defined path regardless of physical wiring. A physical star-ring (IBM token ring, 16 Mbps) wired each node to a MAU, which closed the ring internally — so it is 'ring logic, star wiring.'

cards.q: Describe Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) and FDDI. What are their speeds and key traits?
cards.a: Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) is 4/16 Mbps using token passing for deterministic access, with each station having a 48-bit MAC address — legacy. FDDI is 100 Mbps with dual counter-rotating rings and survived as a campus backbone legacy technology.

cards.q: How does token passing control access in a ring?
cards.a: A small 'token' frame circulates; a station that holds the token may send one frame, then passes the token on. In a single-token ring only one station transmits at a time, giving deterministic access with no collisions.

cards.q: What does a ring monitor / active monitor do in a token ring?
cards.a: It watches for lost tokens and other failures to keep the ring operating.

cards.q: What are the pros and cons of a ring topology?
cards.a: Pros: no collisions thanks to token passing (up to 16 Mbps), deterministic delay for real-time traffic, dual FDDI ring self-heals, and no bandwidth contention under light load. Cons: one break in a single ring takes the whole ring down, nodes are hard to add/remove, it is expensive/complex and not Ethernet, and it is legacy, replaced by switched Ethernet.

cards.q: What media-access method does a ring use, and why can you never mention collisions in a token ring?
cards.a: A ring uses token passing, not CSMA/CD. Because only one station transmits at a time, there are no collisions in a token ring, so mentioning collisions there is wrong.

cards.q: Must a ring be physically wired in a circle?
cards.a: No. The physical layout can be star (each node wired to a MAU that closes the ring internally); only the logic is a ring. Saying 'it must be wired in a circle' is wrong.

cards.q: What happens to a single ring versus a dual ring when there is a break?
cards.a: A single ring halves/splits and goes down on a break, while a dual-ring (FDDI) survives by self-healing using its counter-rotating second ring.

cards.q: Where does ring topology normally appear in modern networks?
cards.a: Ring is a legacy physical/distribution-layer topology; modern switches use STP trees rather than rings. Ring-like path diversity survives in Metro Ethernet rings, which redirect traffic the other way on a fiber cut.

cards.q: In the ring Quick Review, what are the key access, speed, and failure numbers?
cards.a: Access is by token passing (deterministic, one sender at a time). Speeds are 4/16 Mbps for Token Ring and 100 Mbps for FDDI — legacy numbers. Physical wiring is star-type (MAU) with ring logic; a break splits a single ring but dual FDDI self-heals. There are no collisions in a ring versus CSMA/CD shared media.
